Why You’ll Love Our Wiener Schnitzel

It goes with everything. A savory fried cutlet is any easy main to devise a meal around. Serve it with roasted vegetables or a simple salad, make it into a sandwich, or pile it high with a sharp slaw — the possibilities are practically infinite!
Simple and fast. This traditional Austrian dish comes together with simple ingredients in under an hour.

Wiener schnitzel is one of those dishes that always sounded to me like something you could only get in a restaurant. But, much like other famous fried cutlet dishes like chicken Milanese, chicken fried steak, and chicken katsu, it’s actually pretty easy to make at home.
This traditional dish (it’s the national dish of Austria!) relies on a handful of simple ingredients to make a super-tasty cutlet that is much more than the sum of its parts.

Per Austrian law, a true wiener schnitzel must be made from veal, but you can certainly substitute pork (I won’t tell). The thinly pounded cutlets are dredged in a mixture of eggs, lemon juice, and cream before being coated with breadcrumbs and shallow-fried. The result is a delicious savory cutlet with just a hint of bright lemony flavor.

“It’s hard not to love a fried cutlet. These are crispy on the outside, juicy and tender on the inside, and packed with flavor. The ingenious technique is whisking lemon juice into the egg for dredging, as the acidity it adds helps cut through the richness of the meat. I can’t wait to try it the next time I dredge chicken. I love that you can use pork here, as veal can be quite expensive.” —Christine, October 2026

I’ve been working in professional kitchens for almost 20 years. I’m a seasoned recipe developer who has worked on content for many online outlets and for cookbooks from America’s Test Kitchen, Ten Speed Press, Rebel Girls, and Clarkson Potter. I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about the difference between “simple” and “streamlined” when it comes to cooking and making sure my recipes are just as flavorful and satisfying when they’re ready in under an hour as they are when they take all afternoon.
Pork or veal cutlets: Veal is traditional, but pork is a great substitute. If you prefer, you can ask your butcher to cut and pound the cutlets for you.
Flour: All-purpose flour is the base of the three-part dredge.
Lemon juice: Adds a bright, citrusy flavor to the egg mixture the cutlets are dredged in.
Heavy cream: Just a little added to the egg mixture gives the finished breading a touch of creamy flavor.
Fine breadcrumbs: The key to the traditional schnitzel breading. If you only have panko, pulse it a few times in the food processor to get a finer texture.

Prepare the dredge. Spread flour in an even layer on a large plate. Whisk together eggs, lemon juice, and heavy cream in a wide, shallow bowl. Spread breadcrumbs into an even layer in a second shallow bowl.
Coat the cutlets. Season the cutlets all over with salt and pepper. Dredge each cutlet in the flour, egg mixture, and breadcrumbs.
Fry. Heat neutral oil in a large heavy-bottomed skillet. Fry the cutlets in two batches until cooked though and both sides are golden-brown. Serve with lemon wedges and chopped parsley, if desired.
Leftovers can be refrigerated in an airtight container for up to 4 days.
What to Serve with Wiener Schnitzel
The Austrian classic is easy to make at home!
2 tablespoons freshly squeezed lemon juice (1 medium lemon)
1 1/2 to 2 pounds pork or veal cutlets (about 6), pounded about 1/4-inch thick
1 1/2 cups neutral oil, such as vegetable, for frying
Finely chopped fresh parsley leaves, for garnish (optional)

Spread 1/2 cup all-purpose flour out on a large plate. Whisk 2 large eggs, 2 tablespoons lemon juice, and 1 tablespoon heavy cream together in a wide, shallow bowl or pie plate. Spread 1 cup fine, dry breadcrumbs out in a second wide, shallow bowl.

Season 1 1/2 to 2 pounds pork cutlets all over with 1 1/2 teaspoons kosher salt and 1 teaspoon black pepper. Working with one cutlet at a time, dredge each cutlet in the flour until completely coated, then shake off any excess flour. Dip in the egg mixture until completely coated, then shake off any excess. Place in the breadcrumbs and flip until evenly coated. Place on a baking sheet or platter in a single layer.

Heat 1 1/2 cups neutral oil in a 12-inch heavy-bottomed skillet over medium-high heat until 350°F to 360°F. Meanwhile, line a second baking sheet with paper towels, or fit the baking sheet with a wire rack. Heat the oven to 200ºF.

Add half of the cutlets to the hot oil and fry until well-browned on the bottom, 4 to 5 minutes. Flip the cutlets with tongs and fry until well-browned on the second side and the cutlets are cooked through, 4 to 5 minutes more.
Transfer the fried cutlets to the paper towels. Place in the oven to keep warm. Repeat frying the remaining cutlets. Garnish with chopped fresh parsley leaves and serve with lemon wedges if desired.
Storage: Leftovers can be refrigerated in an airtight container for up to 4 days.
